Girdwood Fire Rescue

Wildfire Preparations for 2026 Season



February 2026 Update

For: Girdwood Board of Supervisors and Anchorage Wildland Urban Interface
Community Action Team

To: Wildland Urban Interface Community Action Team (WUICAT), GBOS

From: Michelle Weston, Girdwood Fire Chief

Subject: Girdwood Fire Rescue Wildland 2026 Preparations

______________________________________________________________________

Good afternoon, I wanted to give you a quick update on Girdwood Fire Rescue’s
wildland 2026 season preparations and thank you for advocating for more dedicated
wildfire funding in the Municipality of Anchorage. I was excited and encouraged to see
the recent work done by WUICAT and wanted to share about our fire service area. We
appreciate the leadership and work of the Anchorage Wildfire Division in getting the
2025 CWPP done and implemented.

Background

Girdwood Fire Rescue: Fire Service Area Protection Value: $984,704,946

1098 addresses, 2,393 structures

Current funding for station base staffing during fire season: 4    ISO: 3

Evacuation Police Agency: Whittier Police

Station 41: Engine 41, Rescue 41 (highway extrication), Tenders 41,42,42, Rescue 42
(backcountry equipment), Brush 41, Medics 41 and 42, Boat 41, 3 command SUVs

Adjacent landowners in wildland urban interface: Chugach National Forest, Chugach
State Park, MOA Heritage Land Bank

Bird, Indian, Portage and Crow Creek Road are outside of a MOA Fire Service Area (no
fire protection taxation). Owners are charged a fee for fire service under municipal
ordinance collected by the MOA.

Unique Fire Service Area Challenges

   •  Outside of Fire Service Area: Crow Creek Road neighborhood and abandoned
      campfires on MOA and USFS land
   •  Tourists that do not understand or care about the burning regulations
   •  Evacuation of an area with high short-term rentals: Tourists
   •  Limited law enforcement and fire staffing for immediate life safety evacuations
       with mutual aid 45 minutes away
   •  Forest Fair occurs during high fire danger bringing 8,000 visitors and campers
       into the community

2025 Highlights

   •  Hosted International Association of Fire Chiefs Wildfire Evacuation Workshop for
         fire and law enforcement.
   •  Created 1) Evacuation Polygons and evacuation language for community which
      are now uploaded into EOC notification system. 2) Evacuation Roles and
       Responsibilities matrix for Girdwood and Turnagain Arm Law Enforcement and
     Response Agencies 3) Obtained number of primary and secondary buildings 4)
      Requested multiagency drill for Spring 2025 (other agencies deferred to 2026
     due to workload)
   •  Trained 50% of workforce to Red Card Standard up from 10% from 2024.
   •  Held 3d annual Wildfire Mitigation Day (free chipping) with Girdwood Wildfire
       Partnership: Chugach Electric, Girdwood Parks and Rec, Alaska Wildlife
      Conservation Center, Alaska Division of Forestry and Fire Protection, Anchorage
       Wildfire Division
   •  Participated in Anchorage CWPP work-sessions and touring consultants around
       service area.
   •  Anchorage Wildfire Division gave community Wildfire Rating Sign
   •  CERT team: wildfire evacuation training and evacuation ppe (30 year old wildfire
       jackets) given to CERT and Whittier police
   •  Deployed Brush 41 and Tender 43 to Nenana Complex and Brush 41 to Bear
      Creek Fire for experience; Chief 41 deployed with Alaska Complex Incident
     Management Team to Bear Creek Fire.

2026 Initiatives

Identify wildfire funding

   •  Improve firefighter staffing
   •  Replace 30-year-old equipment and basic ppe: Completed (state grant)
   •  Red card training in Girdwood: Completed (state grant)
   •  Wildfire education and evacuation training for community: NFPA grant submitted
   •  Polaris Ranger 41: Completed (non-taxpayer funding)
   •  Polaris Ranger 42: find funding
   •  Replacement Brush 41 (2007): requested MOA include Brush 41 in MOA wildfire
      defense fund grant application 9/16/2022. Wildfire Division submitting slipin
      replacement grant 2026.
   •  Brush disposal opportunities: find funding

Wildfire Ready Workforce

   •  Target: 100% complete refresher with Anchorage Wildfire Division
   •  Target: 80% of workforce have red card training
   •  Hold Evacuation exercise May/June 2026
   •  Engage CERT, Whittier Police in preparedness efforts
   •  Deployments to increase knowledge and training
   •  Attend IAFC Community Risk Reduction/Wildfire Conference
   •  Train firefighters to do wildfire home assessments
   • REMS module available for deployment

Wildfire Ready Equipment

   •  Place a Polaris Ranger in service with small pump to access trail fires
   •  Modify Brush 41 from lessons learned on 2025 fire deployments
   •  Replace 20+ year old equipment
   •  Provide all firefighters with wildfire ppe

Wildfire Ready Community

   •  Engage and motivate homeowners in defensible space and evacuation
      preparedness and burning regulations
   •  Wildfire psas on Girdwood social media channels, Glacier City Radio and
      Turnagain News, new Girdwood Fire webpage
   •  Incorporate wildfire evacuation knowledge for local employers (Crow Creek Mine,
      Alyeska Resort, Alaska Wildlife Conservation Center)
   •  Engage Girdwood’s nightly rental owners to educate accommodation guests on
      evacuation notifications and burning regulations

Girdwood Wildfire Partnership

Chugach Electric, Girdwood Parks and Rec, Alaska Wildlife Conservation Center,
Alaska Division of Forestry and Fire Protection, Anchorage Wildfire Division

Funding for 2026 Season

$9,998 Grant: Alaska Division of Forestry & Fire Protection

   •  Equipment: helmets, 8 sets of ppe, fedcos (4) and 3 practice shelters
   •  Training: Initial red card training

2026 Funding requests submitted

   •  $10,000 NFPA Grant for evacuation materials, wildfire homeowner education
   •  AFD Wildfire Division is submitting federal grant to replace 30+ year old pump on
      Brush 41 and for UTV slide in unit
   •  No other dedicated funding identified yet for community chipping etc.

We’re so grateful that the boomerang winter has brought
us back to snow! The sun is a little higher in the sky, too!
Remember that the condition under the snow is varied:
overflow and thin ice may be covered, but they’re still
there. Stay mindful of avalanche hazards from above, and
stay up to date on the avalanche conditions, particularly on
trails that cross avalanche runout zones. Chugach
Avalanche Center

The Lower Iditarod has been great for walking, xc skiing
and biking, thanks to Cliff Larsen. The grooming there has
been spectacular and very appreciated. Thanks to all our
volunteer groomers for keeping the trails in as good shape as possible.

Please pick up after your dog.

Year-round staff are now handling trash and mutt-mitt refills. If you
see anything that needs attention, please contact Kyle
kelleykt@muni.org or Margaret tylerms@muni.org.

Currently, the seasonal positions are posted on the MOA hiring site
for the summer Park Caretaker and Trail crew. Seasonal crew from
last year have been invited to reapply.

Thank you to local photographers, Ken Graham and Randy Brandon
for helping staff to acquire negatives to reprint the old Girdwood
photos in the Community Center with fresher renditions.

Trails: Trails Committee is working on updating the winter map and Girdwood Trails
Management Plan. GTC is looking for volunteers to help measure trail segments from specific
points with Gaia app. Reach out to Margaret Tyler if you’re interested in helping. Working on
getting materials ordered to replace the bridge between Crow Creek Road and Townsquare. The
bridge rebuild will be this spring/summer. As well, preparing for the other trail projects that will
take place this summer with getting materials that are needed.

                                  Roads

Road Status: The usual winter continues with weather swings that bring very cold temps and
warmup with heavy rain. The last rain event brought over 3” of precipation that caused minor
flooding and erioson damage on Chyrstal Mountain. The Service Area continues to contract an
additional thaw truck to open drainages and supplement the work that Western is doing to keep
drainages open. Unfortunately, the persistent cold, lack of snow coverage, and constant seep are
creating a relentless overflow cycle, so progress is slow, and thawed areas often re-freeze. The
additional thaw truck is helpful, but expensive. Paying for this slow-moving emergency will
impact available funds for summer projects. Still have two months of pure winter to go, so this
will continue to be a daily challenge for the staff and the service area’s budget for the coming
months. We’re preparing for spring break, but look forward to warmer days and better
conditions. Crews will continue to tackle problems as they arise and keep sanding and plowing
as needed.


                           Major project updates:
Ruane Road fish passage culvert replacement. The Boutet company will lead project
management for this new culvert project, and the Jacobs company will assist in ensuring
compliance with the EPA grant and federal requirements. We will issue a Request for Proposal
(RFP) for Design and engineering services for the new culvert once EPA completes its review
and approves the RFP. This work will finalize the project's complete bid package for
construction. Most likely constructed in summer 2027.

Winner Creek Trail Bridge at Glacier Creek crossing: A complete construction bid package is
out for bid. We’re currently taking questions from potential bidders, and a bid opening is
scheduled for March 12th. We have had good interest in the project from contractors. Working
with the USFS to finalize the understanding that USFS will take over ownership and inspection
of the bridge once the construction partnership of MOA and USFS is completed. USFA has sent
a letter that commits to this partnership and is currently working on a formal agreement. The
project still has a funding gap, according to the professional estimate, but we’re moving forward
with putting the project out to bid to determine the bridge's real construction market value.  If we
end up with a funding gap, we will address it with GBOS once we have more information.

GVSA Road Maintenance contract: The five-year term contract with Western comes to an end at
the end of April. We’re currently working on documents and equipment specifications to send to
the Purchasing department and the contract out to bid in the next month.

  RESOLUTION OF SUPPORT FOR REZONE OF THE “OLD GRAVEL PIT” PARCEL TO SUPPORT
 REMOTE AVALANCHE CONTROL SYSTEMS ALONG THE SEWARD HIGHWAY CORRIDOR AND
TO UPDATE LAND USE CODE FOR THE GIRDWOOD AIRPORT ZONE TO FOLLOW THE INTENT OF
                  THE 2025 GIRDWOOD COMPREHENSIVE PLAN

WHEREAS, the Alaska Dept of Transportation (AKDOT) and the Alaska Railroad have a documented need to update
their avalanche mitigation systems along the Seward Highway corridor; and

WHEREAS, AKDOT has selected a tower based Remote Avalanche Control System (RACS), which will improve the
reliability and efficiency of avalanche mitigation operations; and

WHEREAS, the RACS system requires a facility for seasonal storage of ordinance and a location for helicopter
operations to reload remote RACS towers with explosive cassettes; and

WHEREAS, a parcel of land at the entrance to Girdwood Valley legally described as US Survey 4805 Tract 29B and
known informally as the “Old Gravel Pit” was identified as a suitable location for the RACS support facility; and

WHEREAS, the 2025 Girdwood Comprehensive Plan (GCP) Land Use map identifies this parcel as “Industrial” which is
fully consistent with the planned use; and

WHEREAS, the current Girdwood zoning code in AMC 21.09.040 is not yet in alignment with the 2025 GCP; and

WHEREAS, under current Land Use code, the implementing zone for the proposed use is the GA (Girdwood Airport)
zone; and

WHEREAS, Anchorage Planning Department has proposed a change to AMC 21.09.040 F.8 which broadens the
definition of the GA zone to incorporate the uses described in the 2025 GCP.

THEREFORE the Girdwood Board of Supervisors supports a rezone of this parcel to GA and concurrent update of GA
zoning code to reflect the intent of the 2025 Girdwood Comprehensive Plan

Alaska Department of Transportation & Public Facilities

Safer Seward Highway Project Team

Re: Comments on Draft Environmental Assessment + Safer Seward Highway Project – Rabbit
Creek to Bird Flats

Dear Project Team,

We write to provide formal comments on the Draft Environmental Assessment (EA) for the
proposed Safer Seward Highway project between Rabbit Creek and Bird Flats.

As legislators representing communities directly connected to and affected by this corridor, we
recognize the importance of safety, reliability, and thoughtful infrastructure investment. We also
recognize the Seward Highway’s unique role — not simply as a transportation route, but as one
of Alaska’s most iconic scenic corridors, forming the gateway to the Kenai Peninsula and
running alongside the irreplaceable landscape of Turnagain Arm and the southern edge of
Chugach State Park.

Our communities place a high priority on protecting the character of Turnagain Arm, the quality
of life of adjacent neighborhoods, and the recreational, scenic, and wildlife values that define this
stretch of highway. We are concerned that, as currently proposed, the project risks fundamentally
altering that character in ways that may not be proportional to the demonstrated safety need.

Community and Landscape Impacts

The corridor between Rabbit Creek and Bird Flats is uniquely constrained by steep
mountainsides, the Alaska Railroad, and the tidal flats of Turnagain Arm. It is also home to the
Turnagain Arm Trail and serves as a primary recreational access point to Chugach State Park.

We are concerned that:

    •   Large-scale rock cuts, extended elevated lanes, and substantial widening may
       permanently alter scenic viewsheds that are integral to the experience of residents and
        visitors alike.

•   Relocation or prolonged closure of segments of the Turnagain Arm Trail could diminish
       access to one of the region’s most valued multi-season recreational assets.
    •  Long construction timelines — potentially 15 to 20 years — would create extended
       disruption to communities, recreation, tourism, and wildlife habitat.

The Seward Highway along Turnagain Arm is not a typical rural arterial. It is a defining
landscape feature of Southcentral Alaska. Any redesign must fully account for that distinction.

Proportionality and Alternatives

We respectfully request that the Final EA more clearly demonstrate that the scale of the proposed
four-lane divided highway is proportional to the documented safety challenges in this corridor.

In particular, we encourage:

    •   Clear presentation of absolute crash data and seasonal patterns to ensure that the
        identified solution aligns directly with documented crash causation.
    •   Transparent evaluation of targeted safety interventions — including median barriers, site-
        specific passing lanes, turn improvements, winter-condition treatments, and speed
      management strategies — that may address safety concerns with reduced environmental
      and scenic impact.
    •   Consideration of emerging vehicle technologies that assist drivers and vehicle to vehicle
       coordination to reduce hazards and accidents.
    •   Consideration of phased or modular approaches that allow safety improvements while
       preserving flexibility for future adaptation.

Safety is a shared priority. The question before us is not whether improvements are warranted,
but whether the current proposal represents the least impactful and most context-sensitive
method of achieving those improvements, while also recognizing the opportunity costs of other
forgone projects.

Stewardship of Public Investment

We also note that the project’s cost — currently estimated in excess of $1.4 billion — represents
one of the largest single transportation investments in state history. While funding sources may
be restricted to certain categories of federal aid, large-scale commitments inevitably shape the
department’s long-term capacity, focus, and sequencing of other high-priority safety projects
statewide.

Given limited public resources and ongoing transportation safety needs across Alaska, it is
essential that this project clearly demonstrate measurable safety benefit relative to its scale and
impact.

Moving Forward

We appreciate the extensive technical work that has gone into the Draft EA and the opportunity
to provide comment. We urge the Department to ensure that the Final EA:

    •   Fully accounts for scenic, recreational, and community character impacts,
    •   Clearly demonstrates proportionality between documented safety issues and the selected
        alternative,
    •   Transparently evaluates lower-impact safety configurations, and
    •   Incorporates meaningful responsiveness to public and stakeholder input.

Turnagain Arm is one of Alaska’s defining landscapes. Infrastructure improvements in this
corridor must reflect not only engineering standards, but stewardship of place.

We look forward to continued engagement as this process advances.

Sincerely,

[Names of Undersigned Legislators]
